title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 280
paragraphs: Thus these men defend what they do — which by me is disallowed. But the Egyptians are excessively careful in their observances, both in other matters concerning the sacred rites and also in the following. Egypt, though it borders upon Libya, does not abound greatly in wild animals; but such as they have are all without exception accounted sacred by them, some living with men and others not. If I were to say for what reasons the sacred animals have been thus dedicated, I should fall into discourse about matters pertaining to the gods, of which I most desire not to speak; and what I have actually said, touching lightly upon them, I said only because I was constrained by necessity. About these animals there is a custom of this kind: certain persons have been appointed from among the Egyptians, both men and women, to provide food for each kind of beast separately, and the office descends from father to son. Those who dwell in the various cities perform vows to them thus: when they make a vow to the god to whom the animal belongs, they shave the head of their children — either the whole, or the half, or the third part of it — and then weigh the hair in the balance against silver, and whatever it weighs the man gives to the person in charge of the animals, and she cuts up fish of equal value and gives it as food to the animals. Thus food for their keep has been provided. If anyone kills any of these animals, the penalty, if he did it wilfully, is death; and if without intent, such penalty as the priests may appoint. But whoever kills an ibis or a hawk, whether wilfully or not, must die.
